claims.text: Conventional sintering of lightweight high-entropy alloys typically produces coarser microstructures.
Conventionally sintered lightweight high-entropy alloys have less consistent oxide films.
Optimized SPS processing refines the microstructure into a fine-grained solid solution with enhanced phase uniformity.
The rapid heating and short sintering cycle of SPS limit grain growth.
SPS minimizes the formation of detrimental intermetallic phases.
The SPS-refined microstructure enhances dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases mechanical strength.
Fine, uniform grain boundaries promote the development and stability of a passivating surface oxide layer.
The stable passivating oxide layer enhances corrosion resistance.
The stable surface oxide layer enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
SPS can preserve low density while improving strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to conventional sintering.
SPS-treated samples are predicted to have statistically significantly higher tensile strength than conventionally sintered samples.
SPS-treated samples are predicted to have statistically significantly higher hardness than conventionally sintered samples.
SPS-treated samples are predicted to exhibit higher electrochemical impedance and improved polarization behavior relative to conventionally sintered samples.
SPS-treated samples are predicted to show lower high-temperature oxidation weight gain or thinner oxide scales than conventionally sintered samples.
SPS-treated samples are predicted to have only a minimal density increase relative to the conventional-sintering baseline.
Excessive SPS heat input can cause grain coarsening or intermetallic-phase precipitation.
If SPS causes grain coarsening, intermetallic precipitation, or a significant density increase, the predicted mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation benefits will be lost.
